title: New Jersey Indian Grocery Store Goes Viral as Parval Deal Sparks Sabzi Mandi Frenzy
excerpt: A $1.99-per-pound discount on pointed gourd drew hundreds of shoppers to a new Indian supermarket, with viral videos earning the store the nickname "American Sabzi Mandi."
body:
• A newly opened Indian grocery store in New Jersey drew massive crowds during its grand opening in early July 2026, with viral videos earning it the nickname "American Sabzi Mandi."
  • The rush was triggered by a promotional offer on parval (pointed gourd) priced at $1.99 per pound — far below typical US import prices for the vegetable.
  • Social media reactions ranged from humor and cultural pride to criticism of crowd behavior, with industrialist Harsh Goenka weighing in on civic discipline.
  • The episode underscores the surging demand for large-format Indian supermarkets across the United States as the South Asian diaspora continues to grow.

A Discount on Pointed Gourd Draws Hundreds

A newly opened Indian grocery store in New Jersey became an unlikely viral sensation in early July after its grand opening attracted hundreds of shoppers and turned its aisles into scenes reminiscent of a crowded Indian vegetable market.

The catalyst was a promotional launch-day offer on parval — pointed gourd, a staple across northern and eastern India — priced at $1.99 per pound, according to American Bazaar. That price represented a steep discount from what Indian diaspora shoppers typically pay for the imported vegetable in the United States, where fresh parval supplies are scarce and command premium prices.

Videos circulating on social media showed customers queuing outside the store before it opened, then surging through the doors to crowd the produce section. Checkout lines snaked through packed aisles as shoppers filled carts with the discounted vegetable and other Indian grocery staples, according to Livemint and LatestLY.

The Birth of the "American Sabzi Mandi"

The footage spread rapidly across X, YouTube, and WhatsApp, with viewers comparing the chaotic scenes to bustling sabzi mandis — the open-air vegetable markets found in cities and towns across India. The phrase "American Sabzi Mandi" quickly gained traction online, becoming the dominant shorthand for the viral moment.

"Scenes from the opening of Indian grocery store in New Jersey, where huge crowds of mostly Gujaratis gather to shop."

— @Pradeep_G7, via X

Many on social media drew comparisons to Black Friday sales — except the prized item was not a television or a smartphone but a humble green vegetable central to home-cooked dal and sabzi. The promotional stock was exhausted within a short period, with demand far exceeding the store's expectations, according to LatestLY. No injuries or safety incidents were reported despite the overcrowding.

A Broader Debate Over Civic Behavior

The viral clips sparked a polarized online discussion. Some users celebrated the turnout as evidence of the fierce loyalty Indian diaspora communities maintain toward familiar foods and cultural touchstones. Others criticized the pushing and jostling visible in the footage, arguing that better crowd discipline was warranted.

RPG Group chairman Harsh Goenka weighed in on the broader conversation, urging better civic sense while cautioning that the actions of a small number of individuals should not define the larger Gujarati community, according to American Bazaar.

The debate reflected a tension familiar to diaspora communities: pride in cultural identity and the booming demand for Indian commerce abroad, set against anxieties about how such moments are perceived by a wider audience.

Riding a Wave of Demand

Beyond the viral spectacle, the New Jersey store's grand opening highlighted a broader trend. The Indian grocery retail segment in the United States has expanded rapidly alongside the country's growing South Asian population, now estimated at over 4.8 million. Large-format Indian supermarkets — stocking fresh produce, regional spices, packaged snacks, and familiar household brands — have become anchor institutions in diaspora hubs across New Jersey, Texas, California, and the greater Chicago area.

For many shoppers, these stores fill a gap that mainstream American supermarkets cannot. Vegetables like parval, tinda, and karela; regional brands of atta and dal; and specialty items for festivals and religious observances are often unavailable at conventional grocery chains. The enthusiastic response to the New Jersey opening illustrates how significant that demand remains, Livemint reported.

What Comes Next

The episode has become another example of how promotional pricing and social media can transform routine retail events into cultural flashpoints. While the identity of the specific store has not been central to the online conversation, the "American Sabzi Mandi" moment has renewed interest in the expanding footprint of Indian grocery retail in the United States.

For the Indian diaspora, the crowded aisles of a New Jersey supermarket carried a message that went well beyond a deal on pointed gourd: the community's appetite for a taste of home shows no signs of slowing down.
